text:
Storyline

Question and evidence
Overall spatial structure and conflict composition
Monthly movement and emerging patterns
Hotspot trajectories and priorities
Implications and limitations

title: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
Research question

Where does recorded armed conflict form unusual local concentrations, how do those concentrations change through time, and which priorities survive alternative analytical choices?



87,103
recorded ACLED events


330
Myanmar townships


57
monthly periods


The study covers January 2021 to September 2025. Results describe recorded event concentration at township scale and support screening for peace-building priorities.

title: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
Study design and data quality


Inputs

ACLED event dates, types, coordinates and fatalities
MIMU Admin-3 township boundaries, P-code v9.4
Projected analysis in EPSG:32646

Conflict dimensions

All recorded events
Battles
Violence against civilians


Quality gates

Validated township geometry and P-code uniqueness
Spatially assigned missing or inconsistent township names
Preserved all township-month combinations, including zero-event months
Audited date and coordinate precision

Only 9 event points remained spatially unmatched. This produces a complete 330 × 57 space-time cube.

title: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
Analytical approach


1. Local structure
Local Moran’s I separates clusters from spatial outliers.
Local Gi* identifies significant high- and low-value concentrations.

2. Temporal development
Monthly Gi* maps reveal movement hidden by total-period aggregation.
Mann-Kendall trends and EHSA classify evolving hotspot behaviour.

3. Interpretation
The 12-month HCSA comparison reveals movement before EHSA classifies each 57-month trajectory.

All permutation procedures use seed 626 and 99 simulations. Nominal p < 0.05 follows the course workflow; BH-adjusted counts provide a stricter sensitivity check.

title: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
Overall concentration is local



34 High-High clusters and 4 Low-High outliers show that neighbouring similarity and local contrast coexist.


Fixed-distance Gi* identifies 78 hotspots and 148 cold spots. The 185.8 km support reveals broad regional concentration.

The two statistics answer different questions: LISA detects similarity and outliers; Gi* identifies concentrations of high or low recorded counts.

title: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
Hotspot geography moves through time

The latest 12 months show repeated concentration in the central dry zone alongside shorter peripheral episodes. April 2023 has the widest study-period spread, with 30 hotspot townships.
Salingyi, Monywa, Pale and Singu appear as hotspots in seven of the latest twelve months; Pakokku, Myaing, Budalin and Yesagyo appear in six.

title: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
EHSA separates four hotspot trajectories





13 oscillating: repeated spatial reversals across several regions
11 sporadic: intermittent concentration without one continuous run
7 intensifying: rising Gi* trajectories in separated Shan, Tanintharyi and Yangon settings
3 diminishing: declining relative concentration in Chipwi, Myitkyina and Pyay

The classification map and monthly profiles are read together because each class compresses a 57-month sequence.

title: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
section: Value-added: priorities robust to model choice
text:
Value-added: priorities robust to model choice




The sensitivity analysis compares:

all events, battles and violence against civilians;
fixed-distance, Queen and symmetric KNN weights;
nine hotspot decisions per township.

26 townships receive at least six votes. 9 townships receive all nine votes.
The strongest agreement forms a central dry-zone corridor across Sagaing and Magway, with additional southern cases in Tanintharyi.

This majority rule is a stability summary. It gives stronger priority evidence than any single model and remains separate from formal combined inference.

title: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
Peace-building priorities


Sustained review
Prioritise repeatedly observed monthly hotspots because their concentration recurs across several recent panels.
Track intensifying hotspots closely because local concentration is rising through time.

Adaptive monitoring
Use event-triggered review for sporadic and oscillating hotspots because concentration reappears without a stable continuous path.
Verify diminishing hotspots in current field conditions because declining relative concentration does not establish low harm.

Operational decisions should combine these screening results with population exposure, displacement, access conditions and consultation with affected communities.

title: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
Limitations and reproducibility


Limits of inference

ACLED coverage reflects reporting access and source availability.
Township aggregation and monthly bins shape the detected pattern.
Event counts measure recorded burden rather than population risk.
The analysis identifies concentration and trend, not causes.


Statistical caution

With 99 permutations, the smallest simulated p-value is about 0.01.
BH adjustment across 330 townships is therefore resolution-limited.
Weight models encode different spatial supports.
Fixed-distance and Queen weights represent different spatial supports.


The Quarto report runs end-to-end and records data sources, CRS, seed, analytical parameters, package roles and methodological decisions.
Technical report: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
Repository: ISSS626-GEO

title: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
7.5 Monthly hot spot progression
The overall map compresses 57 months into one total. To reveal movement hidden by that aggregation, the next analysis computes Local Gi* separately for every month. It combines the Chapter 10 HCSA map workflow with the Chapter 6 monthly small-multiple layout. Queen contiguity preserves immediate township adjacency and avoids the broad smoothing created by Myanmar’s large critical distance.


Show code
set.seed(626)

conflict_nb <- conflict_st %>%
  activate("geometry") %>%
  mutate(
    nb = include_self(st_contiguity(geometry)),
    wt = st_weights(nb, style = "W", allow_zero = TRUE),
    .before = 1
  ) %>%
  set_nbs("nb") %>%
  set_wts("wt")

gi_stars <- conflict_nb %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  mutate(
    gi_star = local_gstar_perm(
      event_count,
      nb,
      wt,
      nsim = 99,
      zero.policy = TRUE
    )
  ) %>%
  tidyr::unnest(gi_star) %>%
  mutate(
    p_sim_fdr = p.adjust(p_sim, method = "BH"),
    monthly_hotspot = factor(
      if_else(p_sim < 0.05 & gi_star > 0, "Hot spot", "Not a hot spot"),
      levels = c("Not a hot spot", "Hot spot")
    )
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

gi_stars %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  summarise(
    township_months = n(),
    nominal_hotspot_months = sum(monthly_hotspot == "Hot spot"),
    fdr_significant_months = sum(p_sim_fdr < 0.05 & gi_star > 0, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  kable()

section: 7.4 Do conflict dimensions point to the same places?
text:
7.4 Do conflict dimensions point to the same places?
The aggregate count can hide whether a hotspot reflects armed confrontation, direct violence against civilians, or both. The next comparison holds the Queen neighbourhood, permutation count, and significance threshold constant, changing only the conflict variable. This makes differences across the three maps substantively interpretable.


Show code
set.seed(626)

dimension_variables <- tibble(
  dimension = c("All events", "Battles", "Violence against civilians"),
  variable = c("event_count", "battle_count", "civilian_count"),
  key = c("all_events", "battles", "civilian_violence")
)

dimension_nb <- include_self(
  st_contiguity(st_geometry(township_totals))
)
dimension_wt <- st_weights(
  dimension_nb,
  style = "W",
  allow_zero = TRUE
)

dimension_gistar <- pmap_dfr(
  dimension_variables,
  function(dimension, variable, key) {
    local_gstar_perm(
      township_totals[[variable]],
      dimension_nb,
      dimension_wt,
      nsim = 99,
      zero.policy = TRUE
    ) %>%
      transmute(
        TS_PCODE = township_totals$TS_PCODE,
        dimension,
        key,
        gi_star,
        p_sim,
        is_hotspot = p_sim < 0.05 & gi_star > 0,
        hotspot_status = factor(
          if_else(is_hotspot, "Hot spot", "Not a hot spot"),
          levels = c("Not a hot spot", "Hot spot")
        )
      )
  }
)

dimension_gistar %>%
  count(dimension, hotspot_status) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = hotspot_status,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0

  kable()

Show code
conflict_hotspot_agreement <- dimension_gistar %>%
  select(TS_PCODE, key, is_hotspot) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = key,
    values_from = is_hotspot
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    agreement_class = case_when(
      all_events & battles & civilian_violence ~ "Shared hotspot",
      battles & civilian_violence ~ "Battle-civilian overlap",
      battles & !civilian_violence ~ "Battle-led hotspot",
      civilian_violence & !battles ~ "Civilian-harm hotspot",
      all_events ~ "Aggregate-only hotspot",
      TRUE ~ "No significant hotspot"
    ),
    agreement_class = factor(
      agreement_class,
      levels = c(
        "No significant hotspot",
        "Aggregate-only hotspot",
        "Battle-led hotspot",
        "Civilian-harm hotspot",
        "Battle-civilian overlap",
        "Shared hotspot"
      )
    )
  )

conflict_hotspot_map <- township_totals %>%
  left_join(conflict_hotspot_agreement, by = "TS_PCODE")

conflict_hotspot_summary <- conflict_hotspot_map %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(agreement_class != "No significant hotspot") %>%
  group_by(agreement_class) %>%
  summarise(
    townships = n(),
    leading_states = paste(
      names(head(sort(table(ST), decreasing = TRUE), 3)),
      collapse = ", "
    ),
    .groups = "drop"

title: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
text:
Public-safety and peace-building implications


Sustained review
Prioritise repeatedly observed monthly hotspots because their concentration recurs across several recent panels.
Track intensifying hotspots closely because local concentration is rising through time.

Adaptive monitoring
Use event-triggered review for sporadic and oscillating hotspots because concentration reappears without a stable continuous path.
Verify diminishing hotspots in current field conditions because declining relative concentration does not establish low harm.

Operational decisions should combine these screening results with population exposure, displacement, access conditions and consultation with affected communities.

title: Market Area Analysis for Retail and Service Locations using Huff model
text:
Market area analysis (also known as Trade Area Analysis) is the process of defining and studying the geographical area from which a business draws its customers. It involves analysing data on consumer demographics, spending habits and competitors to understand market viability, identify opportunities, and inform decisions about location, marketing and expansion. It often combines empirical observation, such as customer spotting, with mathematical models to identify market segments and understand customer behaviour.
The Huff model is a geospatial analysis method commonly used in market area analysis. It predicts the probability that a consumer from a specific area will patronise a particular store, based on the store’s attractiveness and its distance relative to competitors. It calculates a store’s market share from attractiveness (e.g. size or sales) and distance or travel time, and the probability decreases as distance or competition increases. This helps businesses assess potential revenue, define trade areas, and make informed decisions about site selection.






NoteMy understanding: where the Huff model sits (Lesson 8)



Lesson 8 introduces the Huff model through a sequence of spatial-interaction ideas:

Spatial interaction needs complementarity (demand at the origin, supply at the destination), transferability (the trip must be affordable), and no intervening opportunity (a closer store offering the same thing would capture the customer first).
Reilly’s law (1931) finds a single breaking point between two centres. Every customer is assigned to exactly one centre, so the trade-area boundaries are hard lines.
Huff (1963) turns this into a probability. A customer in village \(i\) can go to any store \(j\), with

\[
U_{ij} = A_j^{\alpha}\, d_{ij}^{-\lambda}, \qquad
p_{ij} = \frac{U_{ij}}{\sum_{k} U_{ik}}
\]
so the trade area becomes a continuous probability surface, and the trade areas of neighbouring stores overlap. - Expected customers follow as \(E_{ij} = p_{ij} \times C_i\) (where \(C_i\) is the market potential, here population), store totals as \(T_j = \sum_i E_{ij}\), and market share as \(M_j = T_j / \sum T_j\). - MCI (Nakanishi and Cooper) generalises the attractiveness term to several weighted variables and estimates the weights from observed shares. Huff with assumed parameters is the simpler, uncalibrated version.




In this hands-on exercise, I gain hands-on experience in performing market area analysis using the Huff model of the MCI package. By the end of this exercise, I will be able:

to import GIS data into R and save them as simple feature data frames using appropriate functions of the sf package;
to import aspatial data into R;
to clean and tidy the data sets so that they are ready for the analysis;
to compute a distance matrix between the origins (i.e. villages) and destinations (i.e. stores);
to compute interaction probabilities using the Huff model; and
to visualise the market area using the tmap and ggplot2 packages.




A fast-food franchise is a business model in which an individual (the franchisee) acquires the rights to operate a restaurant under an established brand owned by a franchisor. This arrangement typically involves franchise fees and adherence to standardised operational procedures. Key considerations before investing include the size of the initial capital outlay, the strength of the brand, and the strategic importance of store location.
In this exercise, I take the role of a data analyst in the business development team of a fast-food franchise. The objective is to delineate the trade areas of existing stores in Taichung City and to produce spatial maps to support market analysis and strategic decision-making.



Four data sets are used in this hands-on exercise:
Geospatial data

STORES_TC: store locations in ESRI shapefile format.
TOWN_TC: town (district) boundaries in ESRI shapefile format.
VILLAGE_TC: village boundaries in ESRI shapefile format.

Aspatial data

pop2019.csv: population data of Taichung City in 2019. H_CNT, P_CNT, M_CNT and F_CNT are the number of households, total population, male population and female population respectively.
Store_sales_data.csv: store sales data.





The R packages needed for this exercise are:

sf for handling geospatial data and performing geoprocessing functions such as computing a distance matrix,
MCI for performing Huff and MCI modelling,
tidyverse for performing data science tasks, including visualisation,
ggstatsplot, an extension of ggplot2 that combines data visualisation with statistical analysis, so that plots show statistical test results directly, and
tmap for plotting cartographic-quality thematic maps.

The code chunk below installs and loads these R packages into the RStudio environment.

pacman::p_load(sf, tidyverse, MCI, tmap, ggstatsplot)

TipMy observation




All three layers are in TWD97 / TM2 zone 121, a projected CRS measured in metres. This matters a lot for the Huff model, because distance enters the formula directly as \(d_{ij}^{-\lambda}\). If one layer were in longitude/latitude, st_distance() would mix up units and the probabilities would be wrong without any error message.
There are 28 stores (points), 28 towns and 622 villages (polygons). The villages will be the origins (where demand lives) and the stores the destinations.
Taichung City actually has 29 districts, but TOWN_TC has only 28. The mountainous Heping District is not included in the boundary data. This shows up again later, when some population records cannot be joined.

TipMy observation



Zooming around the interactive map:

The stores are not evenly spread. About half of them cluster in the old city core and the Xitun/Nantun area, a few are in the western coastal towns (e.g. WJ, SA), and the rest are single stores in outer districts such as TG (Dajia), OL (Houli), EH (Dongshi) and WF (Wufeng).
The villages are very small in the city centre and very large in the rural and hilly districts. Village size tracks population density, so the large rural polygons look important on the map but hold relatively few people.
I expect the outer stores to have large but thinly populated trade areas, and the core stores to have small, overlapping ones. The Huff results below test this.

Store_size = 100 for every store. This is the key assumption of the teaching example (see the note below).









NoteMy understanding: what Store_size = 100 means for the model



In the Huff formula, attractiveness enters as \(A_j^{\alpha}\). When every store has the same \(A_j\), this term is identical in the numerator and in every term of the denominator, so it cancels out:
\[
p_{ij} = \frac{100 \cdot d_{ij}^{-2}}{\sum_k 100 \cdot d_{ik}^{-2}} = \frac{d_{ij}^{-2}}{\sum_k d_{ik}^{-2}}
\]
So in this exercise the model is driven only by distance and by where the competitors are. Any difference between stores in the results comes from location, not from size, brand or service quality. To make attractiveness matter, I would replace Store_size with a real variable such as floor area, seats, or a drive-through flag.

TipMy observation



The two sides of the join mismatch have different causes:

5 polygons with no population. Their codes end in S01-S03 (e.g. 66000120S01) and they have no village name. They are special non-village units in Qingshui, Wuqi and Longjing, covering the coastal port and air-base area, so they have no registered residents. Removing them is correct and loses no demand. They show up as white gaps on the trade-area map later.
8 population records with no polygon. All 8 are villages in Heping District (about 10,900 residents), the district missing from the boundary layer. These residents are left out of the model.

After filtering, 617 villages remain as demand origins and all four count fields are complete. Leaving out Heping is a small, documented under-count. It is also reasonable for this question, since Heping is mountain terrain far from any store.






Instead of calculating the distance between the village polygons and the stores, we calculate a representative point for each village using the code chunk below. Then we compute the distance between these village points and the stores.

village_center <- st_point_on_surface(village)
distmat <- st_distance(village_center, stores)







NoteMy understanding: st_point_on_surface() vs st_centroid()



The lecture text calls these points “centroids”, but the code uses st_point_on_surface(). The two are not the same:

st_centroid() gives the geometric centre, which can fall outside a concave or multi-part polygon (for example a crescent-shaped village).
st_point_on_surface() always returns a point inside the polygon.

When I checked this data, 8 villages had a true centroid lying outside their own boundary, and the largest shift between the two points was about 1.4 km. With a \(d^{-2}\) decay, moving a village’s origin by a kilometre near a store can change its probability a lot, so point-on-surface is the safer choice.


Next, the code chunk below converts the distance matrix into a long data.frame format.

rownames(distmat) <- village$`VILLCODE`
colnames(distmat) <- stores$`Store_CD`

distmat_long <- distmat %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column(var = "VILLCODE") %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -VILLCODE,
               names_to = "Store_CD",
               values_to = "distance") %>%
  mutate(distance = as.numeric(distance))







TipMy observation




distmat is a 617 × 28 matrix (villages × stores), so distmat_long has 617 × 28 = 17,276 rows, one for every village-store pair. The Huff model needs every pair because every store competes for every village.
st_distance() returns values with a units attribute (m). The final mutate(distance = as.numeric(distance)) drops the unit, because MCI needs plain numbers.
These are straight-line distances. Real customers travel on roads, so a road-network distance or travel time would be more realistic, especially across rivers and hills.






The code chunk below builds the interaction matrix required by the MCI package.

interaction_matrix <- distmat_long %>%
  left_join(stores %>%
              st_drop_geometry() %>%
              select(Store_CD, Store_size),
            by = "Store_CD") %>%
  relocate(distance, .after = last_col())

The shortest village-store distance is about 108 m (a village with a store inside it) and the longest is about 41 km. The median is about 12 km. That median says little about customer behaviour, though: a resident does not travel to the median store, and under the Huff model it is the nearest few stores that matter.
Store_size is constant at 100, so it confirms the attractiveness term will cancel out.







huff_share <- huff.shares(interaction_matrix,
                          "VILLCODE",
                          "Store_CD",
                          "Store_size",
                          "distance")







NoteMy understanding: what huff.shares() does



Reading the function’s source code, huff.shares():

sorts the data by origin and destination;
computes the utility \(U_{ij} = A_j^{\gamma} \times d_{ij}^{\lambda}\) with the default gamma = 1 and lambda = -2. MCI writes the negative sign inside \(\lambda\), while the lecture slide writes \(d^{-\lambda}\) with \(\lambda = 2\). They are the same model;
sums \(U_{ij}\) for each origin to get sum_U_ij; and
returns p_ij = U_ij / sum_U_ij.

So, for every village, the 28 probabilities add up to exactly 1. This is the “logical consistency” requirement in the slides (\(0 < p_{ij} < 1\) and \(\sum_j p_{ij} = 1\)).
Two consequences I noticed:

Because the distance decay is a power function, the distance unit does not matter. Changing metres to kilometres multiplies all of a village’s distances by the same constant, which cancels in \(p_{ij}\). With an exponential decay (dtype = "exp"), the unit would matter.
huff.shares() checks its input with exists(...), so the first argument must be a named object such as interaction_matrix. It does not work if a pipe result is passed into it directly.





First, we select the market share data of one store using the Store_CD field (i.e. BT).

market_share <- huff_share %>%
  filter(Store_CD == "BT")

Next, the trade area of the selected store is derived using the code chunk below.

Trade_area <- village %>%
  left_join(market_share)

Before plotting the trade area map, the code chunk below extracts the selected store from the stores sf data.frame.

selected_store <- stores %>%
  filter(Store_CD == "BT")

Now, the code chunk below plots the trade area of the selected store.

tm_shape(Trade_area) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "p_ij",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 10,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Patronage Probability")) +
  tm_shape(selected_store) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.3,
          fill = "red",
          col = "black") +
  tm_title("Distribution of Patronage Probability of Store BT by village") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2)














TipMy observation




BT’s trade area is a probability surface, not a boundary. The darkest class forms a compact core around the store in Beitun and fades outward. No village has a probability of exactly 0. Even villages 30+ km away keep a small share, which is what “probabilistic” means in Huff’s definition of a trade area.
The surface is not circular. It is shaped by the competitors. The white holes are not simply the villages furthest from BT. They are the villages right next to other stores: the coastal stores in the west, TG in the north, and the stores south of the city centre. There, the nearby competitor takes almost all the demand and BT drops to about 0. BT’s core extends much further east into the Beitun, Taiping and Xinshe foothills, because there are few other stores in that direction.
Far-away villages are not the lowest. Villages at the northern and southern edges sit in the middle classes (about 0.02-0.03), close to the 1/28 ≈ 0.036 that BT would get if all stores were equally far away. When every store is far, the distances become similar and the probabilities spread out evenly. A village next to a competitor gives BT much less than a remote village does.
Read the quantile legend carefully. With style = "quantile" and n = 10, each colour class holds about 62 villages regardless of the values. Nine classes are squeezed between 0 and 0.067, while the top class spans 0.068-0.944. The map is good for ranking villages, but it makes BT’s influence look much larger than it is. Only about 10% of villages give BT more than 0.07. With fixed breaks (e.g. 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4), only a handful of villages around the store would look dark.
Comparing stores. BT has close competitors: DT about 1.5 km away, and TY and DK both within about 2.3 km. When I changed "BT" to "TG" (the Dajia store in the northwest), the picture was very different. TG has no nearby competitor, so villages up to about 5 km away still give it more than 0.4. BT has a contested trade area, while TG has a captive one. A simple buffer of the same radius around each store would hide this difference.






One use of the Huff model is to estimate store sales from village population. First, we append the P_CNT field from the village sf data.frame to the huff_share data.frame using the code chunk below.

huff_share_pp <- huff_share %>%
  left_join(village %>%
              st_drop_geometry() %>%
              select(VILLCODE, P_CNT),
            by = "VILLCODE") %>%
  relocate(distance, .after = last_col())

Next, shares.total() of the MCI package is used to calculate the total sales, using the code chunk below.

huff_total <- shares.total(huff_share_pp,
                           "VILLCODE",
                           "Store_CD",
                           "p_ij",
                           "P_CNT")







NoteMy understanding: what shares.total() returns



shares.total() implements the slide formulas \(E_{ij} = p_{ij} \times C_i\) and \(T_j = \sum_i E_{ij}\), with \(C_i\) = P_CNT. The output has one row per store:

sum_E_j: the expected number of customers \(T_j\) allocated to that store;
share_j: its market share \(M_j = T_j / \sum T_j\).

Every resident of the 617 villages is allocated to some store, so sum(sum_E_j) equals the total modelled population (about 2.80 million). Strictly speaking, these are expected customers, not sales in dollars. Comparing them with Total_Sales therefore assumes that each resident spends roughly the same amount.


The code chunk below appends the estimated store sales (\(E_j\)) onto the stores sf data.frame.

store_sales_est <- stores %>%
  left_join(huff_total,
            by = join_by("Store_CD" == "suppliers_single"))

Now, we can visualise how well the estimated sales compare with the actual sales using the code chunk below.

store_sales_nongeom <- store_sales_est %>%
  st_drop_geometry()


ggscatterstats(store_sales_nongeom,
               x = sum_E_j,
               y = Total_Sales)














TipMy observation




The relationship is positive and significant: \(\hat r_{Pearson} \approx 0.58\), 95% CI [0.26, 0.78], p ≈ 0.001, with 28 stores. Stores that the model allocates more residents to do tend to sell more.
But location explains only about a third of the variation (\(r^2 \approx 0.33\)). This is expected, because the model only knows distance and competition. Attractiveness is fixed at 100, and \(\lambda\) is not calibrated.
The points below the line are mostly the outer stores. TG (Dajia), SQ (Shengang), ZS (Taiping) and EH (Dongshi) sell much less than their modelled customer totals. The Huff model is a closed system: every resident must choose one of the 28 stores. A lone store in a large rural area is therefore credited with everyone there, even though many of those people will not travel 5-10 km for fast food or will choose another brand. This is the main structural weakness I see in the model.
The points above the line are mostly in the western and central city, e.g. DD (Longjing, toward the industrial park and Tunghai University) and ZK (the Zhong Ke store in Xitun, named after the Central Taiwan Science Park). These areas attract many daytime workers and students, who are not counted in residential P_CNT.
QH is a central store that also sits well below the line, and it has the lowest average bill. This points to a format or operational issue rather than location.

Business takeaway: the gap between observed and modelled sales is more useful than the correlation itself. It separates “poor location” from “good location, weak performance”, and it suggests that daytime population would be a better demand measure than residential population for some stores.


The code chunk below reshapes the Huff probabilities into a wide village-by-store table.

huff_share_wider <- huff_share %>%
  select(VILLCODE, Store_CD, p_ij) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Store_CD,
              values_from = p_ij)







TipMy observation



huff_share_wider is a 617 × 29 table: VILLCODE plus one column per store. Each row adds up to 1. This format is easy to share with a business team, because each row shows how one village’s demand is split across all 28 stores. It also makes it easy to find each village’s dominant store (the column with the highest probability). With equal attractiveness, the dominant store is always the nearest store, so the dominant-store map is effectively a Voronoi diagram of the stores.












NoteWhere competition is strongest



From huff_share_wider, I calculated how evenly each village’s probability is spread across stores, using the effective number of competitors \(1/\sum_j p_{ij}^2\). The result surprised me:

Villages right next to a store, even in the dense city core, are close to 1. A store a few hundred metres away gets almost all of that village’s demand under \(d^{-2}\).
The most split villages are in the gaps between stores and across the rural periphery. When every store is far away, the distances are similar, so no single store dominates.

For expansion, these peripheral villages are unclaimed demand: a new store there would become the nearest store and capture most of it. A new store in the core would mostly take customers from other stores in the same franchise.








NoteIs λ = 2 the right distance decay?



The lecture uses MCI’s default lambda = -2, but Lesson 8 stresses that the Huff model should be calibrated. Re-running huff.shares() with different lambda values and comparing modelled shares (share_j) with observed sales shares:

The share error (RMSE) is lowest at about λ = 1, with the default λ = 2 slightly worse.
Larger λ (stronger decay) makes the fit clearly worse, because it gives the isolated outer stores even more of their surrounding villages.

This suggests fast-food customers in Taichung are less distance-sensitive than λ = 2 assumes. One reason could be that people buy near work, school or on the way home, not only near where they live.
This is only a rough check (28 stores, revenue standing in for customers). A proper MCI calibration would regress observed village-level shares on distance and attractiveness after the log-centering transformation. The POD code field in the sales data is a delivery zone, not a village code, so village-level shares cannot be rebuilt from this data.












Question
What I learned




What is a Huff trade area?
A continuous probability surface. Trade areas of neighbouring stores overlap, unlike the hard boundaries of Reilly’s law.


What drives the result here?
Only distance and competition. Store_size = 100 cancels out of \(p_{ij}\).


Why check the joins?
The sales file is national. The 5 dropped polygons are non-residential special units, and the 8 unmatched population records are Heping District, which is missing from the boundary layer.


How good is the model?
r ≈ 0.58 with observed sales. It over-credits isolated outer stores and under-credits stores near campuses and workplaces.


What would improve it?
Real attractiveness variables, road travel time instead of straight-line distance, daytime population, and a λ calibrated with MCI on observed shares.







Kam, T. S. R for Geospatial Data Science and Analytics, Chapter 18: Market Area Analysis for Retail and Service Locations using Huff model.
ISSS626 Lesson 8: Market Area Analysis for Retail and Service Locations: Huff and MCI Models.
Huff, D. L. (1963). A Probabilistic Analysis of Shopping Center Trade Areas. Land Economics, 39(1), 81-90.
Nakanishi, M. and Cooper, L. G. (1982). Simplified Estimation Procedures for MCI Models. Marketing Science, 1(3), 314-322.
Wieland, T. (2017). Market Area Analysis for Retail and Service Locations with MCI. The R Journal, 9(1), 298-323.

title: Market Area Analysis for Retail and Service Locations using Huff model
text:
Market area analysis (also known as Trade Area Analysis) is the process of defining and studying the geographical area from which a business draws its customers. It involves analysing data on consumer demographics, spending habits and competitors to understand market viability, identify opportunities, and inform decisions about location, marketing and expansion. It often combines empirical observation, such as customer spotting, with mathematical models to identify market segments and understand customer behaviour.
The Huff model is a geospatial analysis method commonly used in market area analysis. It predicts the probability that a consumer from a specific area will patronise a particular store, based on the store’s attractiveness and its distance relative to competitors. It calculates a store’s market share from attractiveness (e.g. size or sales) and distance or travel time, and the probability decreases as distance or competition increases. This helps businesses assess potential revenue, define trade areas, and make informed decisions about site selection.






NoteMy understanding: where the Huff model sits (Lesson 8)



Lesson 8 introduces the Huff model through a sequence of spatial-interaction ideas:

Spatial interaction needs complementarity (demand at the origin, supply at the destination), transferability (the trip must be affordable), and no intervening opportunity (a closer store offering the same thing would capture the customer first).
Reilly’s law (1931) finds a single breaking point between two centres. Every customer is assigned to exactly one centre, so the trade-area boundaries are hard lines.
Huff (1963) turns this into a probability. A customer in village \(i\) can go to any store \(j\), with

\[
U_{ij} = A_j^{\alpha}\, d_{ij}^{-\lambda}, \qquad
p_{ij} = \frac{U_{ij}}{\sum_{k} U_{ik}}
\]
so the trade area becomes a continuous probability surface, and the trade areas of neighbouring stores overlap. - Expected customers follow as \(E_{ij} = p_{ij} \times C_i\) (where \(C_i\) is the market potential, here population), store totals as \(T_j = \sum_i E_{ij}\), and market share as \(M_j = T_j / \sum T_j\). - MCI (Nakanishi and Cooper) generalises the attractiveness term to several weighted variables and estimates the weights from observed shares. Huff with assumed parameters is the simpler, uncalibrated version.




In this hands-on exercise, I gain hands-on experience in performing market area analysis using the Huff model of the MCI package. By the end of this exercise, I will be able:

to import GIS data into R and save them as simple feature data frames using appropriate functions of the sf package;
to import aspatial data into R;
to clean and tidy the data sets so that they are ready for the analysis;
to compute a distance matrix between the origins (i.e. villages) and destinations (i.e. stores);
to compute interaction probabilities using the Huff model; and
to visualise the market area using the tmap and ggplot2 packages.




A fast-food franchise is a business model in which an individual (the franchisee) acquires the rights to operate a restaurant under an established brand owned by a franchisor. This arrangement typically involves franchise fees and adherence to standardised operational procedures. Key considerations before investing include the size of the initial capital outlay, the strength of the brand, and the strategic importance of store location.
In this exercise, I take the role of a data analyst in the business development team of a fast-food franchise. The objective is to delineate the trade areas of existing stores in Taichung City and to produce spatial maps to support market analysis and strategic decision-making.



Four data sets are used in this hands-on exercise:
Geospatial data

STORES_TC: store locations in ESRI shapefile format.
TOWN_TC: town (district) boundaries in ESRI shapefile format.
VILLAGE_TC: village boundaries in ESRI shapefile format.

Aspatial data

pop2019.csv: population data of Taichung City in 2019. H_CNT, P_CNT, M_CNT and F_CNT are the number of households, total population, male population and female population respectively.
Store_sales_data.csv: store sales data.

title: Market Area Analysis for Retail and Service Locations using Huff model
text:
The R packages needed for this exercise are:

sf for handling geospatial data and performing geoprocessing functions such as computing a distance matrix,
MCI for performing Huff and MCI modelling,
tidyverse for performing data science tasks, including visualisation,
ggstatsplot, an extension of ggplot2 that combines data visualisation with statistical analysis, so that plots show statistical test results directly, and
tmap for plotting cartographic-quality thematic maps.

The code chunk below installs and loads these R packages into the RStudio environment.

pacman::p_load(sf, tidyverse, MCI, tmap, ggstatsplot)

The output above shows that the three data sets are in the TWD97 / TM2 zone 121 (i.e. EPSG:3826) projected coordinate system.






Important



For any geospatial analysis, it is important to check and confirm that all the geospatial data are in the same projected coordinate system.








TipMy observation




All three layers are in TWD97 / TM2 zone 121, a projected CRS measured in metres. This matters a lot for the Huff model, because distance enters the formula directly as \(d_{ij}^{-\lambda}\). If one layer were in longitude/latitude, st_distance() would mix up units and the probabilities would be wrong without any error message.
There are 28 stores (points), 28 towns and 622 villages (polygons). The villages will be the origins (where demand lives) and the stores the destinations.
Taichung City actually has 29 districts, but TOWN_TC has only 28. The mountainous Heping District is not included in the boundary data. This shows up again later, when some population records cannot be joined.




tmap_mode("view")
tm_shape(town) +
  tm_polygons() +
tm_shape(village) +
  tm_polygons() +
tm_shape(stores) +
  tm_dots()




tmap_mode("plot")







TipMy observation



Zooming around the interactive map:

The stores are not evenly spread. About half of them cluster in the old city core and the Xitun/Nantun area, a few are in the western coastal towns (e.g. WJ, SA), and the rest are single stores in outer districts such as TG (Dajia), OL (Houli), EH (Dongshi) and WF (Wufeng).
The villages are very small in the city centre and very large in the rural and hilly districts. Village size tracks population density, so the large rural polygons look important on the map but hold relatively few people.
I expect the outer stores to have large but thinly populated trade areas, and the core stores to have small, overlapping ones. The Huff results below test this.

The file is not limited to Taichung. It contains about 233 different store codes, so it looks like the franchise’s national sales table, plus some rows with a missing store code. title: Market Area Analysis for Retail and Service Locations using Huff model
text:
The code chunk below aggregates the store sales data by Store Code.

store_sales_aggre <- store_sales %>%
  group_by(`Store Code`) %>%
  summarise(
    "Total_Bill" = sum(Bills, na.rm = TRUE),
    "Total_Sales" = sum(Amount, na.rm = TRUE))




In the code chunk below, left_join() of dplyr is used to append data from the store_sales_aggre data.frame onto the stores sf data.frame. At the same time, a new field called Store_size is created.

stores <- stores %>%
  left_join(store_sales_aggre,
            by = join_by(Store_CD == `Store Code`)) %>%
  mutate(Store_size = 100)

Next, summary() is used to check whether there are any missing values in the data.frame.

TipMy observation




No NAs appear in Total_Bill or Total_Sales, so all 28 stores matched a sales record.
Total sales range from about 1.48 million (EH, Dongshi) to 8.23 million (FH), roughly a 5.6× gap. Total bills range from 1,767 to 14,468, an even larger gap. So the stores differ mainly in how many orders they receive, not in how much each order is worth. That suits the Huff model, which predicts how many customers a store attracts.
Store_size = 100 for every store. This is the key assumption of the teaching example (see the note below).









NoteMy understanding: what Store_size = 100 means for the model



In the Huff formula, attractiveness enters as \(A_j^{\alpha}\). When every store has the same \(A_j\), this term is identical in the numerator and in every term of the denominator, so it cancels out:
\[
p_{ij} = \frac{100 \cdot d_{ij}^{-2}}{\sum_k 100 \cdot d_{ik}^{-2}} = \frac{d_{ij}^{-2}}{\sum_k d_{ik}^{-2}}
\]
So in this exercise the model is driven only by distance and by where the competitors are. Any difference between stores in the results comes from location, not from size, brand or service quality. To make attractiveness matter, I would replace Store_size with a real variable such as floor area, seats, or a drive-through flag.

The output above shows that the village ID (i.e. V_ID) in the pop2019 data.frame does not have the same structure as the village code (VILLCODE) in the village sf data.frame. The code chunk below removes the “-” sign from the values.

pop2019 <- pop2019 %>%
  mutate(V_ID = str_remove_all(V_ID, "-"))

Now we are ready to append the data in the pop2019 data.frame onto the village sf data.frame using left_join() of dplyr.

village <- village %>%
  left_join(pop2019, by = join_by(VILLCODE == V_ID))

TipMy observation



The two sides of the join mismatch have different causes:

5 polygons with no population. Their codes end in S01-S03 (e.g. 66000120S01) and they have no village name. They are special non-village units in Qingshui, Wuqi and Longjing, covering the coastal port and air-base area, so they have no registered residents. Removing them is correct and loses no demand. They show up as white gaps on the trade-area map later.
8 population records with no polygon. All 8 are villages in Heping District (about 10,900 residents), the district missing from the boundary layer. These residents are left out of the model.

After filtering, 617 villages remain as demand origins and all four count fields are complete. Leaving out Heping is a small, documented under-count. It is also reasonable for this question, since Heping is mountain terrain far from any store.

title: Market Area Analysis for Retail and Service Locations using Huff model
text:
Instead of calculating the distance between the village polygons and the stores, we calculate a representative point for each village using the code chunk below. Then we compute the distance between these village points and the stores.

village_center <- st_point_on_surface(village)
distmat <- st_distance(village_center, stores)







NoteMy understanding: st_point_on_surface() vs st_centroid()



The lecture text calls these points “centroids”, but the code uses st_point_on_surface(). The two are not the same:

st_centroid() gives the geometric centre, which can fall outside a concave or multi-part polygon (for example a crescent-shaped village).
st_point_on_surface() always returns a point inside the polygon.

When I checked this data, 8 villages had a true centroid lying outside their own boundary, and the largest shift between the two points was about 1.4 km. With a \(d^{-2}\) decay, moving a village’s origin by a kilometre near a store can change its probability a lot, so point-on-surface is the safer choice.


Next, the code chunk below converts the distance matrix into a long data.frame format.

rownames(distmat) <- village$`VILLCODE`
colnames(distmat) <- stores$`Store_CD`

distmat_long <- distmat %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column(var = "VILLCODE") %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -VILLCODE,
               names_to = "Store_CD",
               values_to = "distance") %>%
  mutate(distance = as.numeric(distance))







TipMy observation




distmat is a 617 × 28 matrix (villages × stores), so distmat_long has 617 × 28 = 17,276 rows, one for every village-store pair. The Huff model needs every pair because every store competes for every village.
st_distance() returns values with a units attribute (m). The final mutate(distance = as.numeric(distance)) drops the unit, because MCI needs plain numbers.
These are straight-line distances. Real customers travel on roads, so a road-network distance or travel time would be more realistic, especially across rivers and hills.

title: Market Area Analysis for Retail and Service Locations using Huff model
text:
The code chunk below builds the interaction matrix required by the MCI package.

interaction_matrix <- distmat_long %>%
  left_join(stores %>%
              st_drop_geometry() %>%
              select(Store_CD, Store_size),
            by = "Store_CD") %>%
  relocate(distance, .after = last_col())


summary(interaction_matrix)

      VILLCODE          Store_CD       Store_size     distance      
 Length   :17276   Length   :17276   Min.   :100   Min.   :  108.5  
 N.unique :  617   N.unique :   28   1st Qu.:100   1st Qu.: 6678.7  
 N.blank  :    0   N.blank  :    0   Median :100   Median :11965.3

TipMy observation




The interaction matrix is in the long “origin-destination” format that huff.shares() expects: one row per pair, with the origin ID, destination ID, attractiveness and distance.
The shortest village-store distance is about 108 m (a village with a store inside it) and the longest is about 41 km. The median is about 12 km. That median says little about customer behaviour, though: a resident does not travel to the median store, and under the Huff model it is the nearest few stores that matter.
Store_size is constant at 100, so it confirms the attractiveness term will cancel out.

title: Market Area Analysis for Retail and Service Locations using Huff model
text:
huff_share <- huff.shares(interaction_matrix,
                          "VILLCODE",
                          "Store_CD",
                          "Store_size",
                          "distance")







NoteMy understanding: what huff.shares() does



Reading the function’s source code, huff.shares():

sorts the data by origin and destination;
computes the utility \(U_{ij} = A_j^{\gamma} \times d_{ij}^{\lambda}\) with the default gamma = 1 and lambda = -2. MCI writes the negative sign inside \(\lambda\), while the lecture slide writes \(d^{-\lambda}\) with \(\lambda = 2\). They are the same model;
sums \(U_{ij}\) for each origin to get sum_U_ij; and
returns p_ij = U_ij / sum_U_ij.

So, for every village, the 28 probabilities add up to exactly 1. This is the “logical consistency” requirement in the slides (\(0 < p_{ij} < 1\) and \(\sum_j p_{ij} = 1\)).
Two consequences I noticed:

Because the distance decay is a power function, the distance unit does not matter. Changing metres to kilometres multiplies all of a village’s distances by the same constant, which cancels in \(p_{ij}\). With an exponential decay (dtype = "exp"), the unit would matter.
huff.shares() checks its input with exists(...), so the first argument must be a named object such as interaction_matrix. It does not work if a pipe result is passed into it directly.





First, we select the market share data of one store using the Store_CD field (i.e. BT).

market_share <- huff_share %>%
  filter(Store_CD == "BT")

Next, the trade area of the selected store is derived using the code chunk below.

Trade_area <- village %>%
  left_join(market_share)

Before plotting the trade area map, the code chunk below extracts the selected store from the stores sf data.frame.

selected_store <- stores %>%
  filter(Store_CD == "BT")

Now, the code chunk below plots the trade area of the selected store.

tm_shape(Trade_area) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "p_ij",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 10,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Patronage Probability")) +
  tm_shape(selected_store) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.3,
          fill = "red",
          col = "black") +
  tm_title("Distribution of Patronage Probability of Store BT by village") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2)














TipMy observation




BT’s trade area is a probability surface, not a boundary. The darkest class forms a compact core around the store in Beitun and fades outward. No village has a probability of exactly 0. Even villages 30+ km away keep a small share, which is what “probabilistic” means in Huff’s definition of a trade area.
The surface is not circular. It is shaped by the competitors. The white holes are not simply the villages furthest from BT. They are the villages right next to other stores: the coastal stores in the west, TG in the north, and the stores south of the city centre. There, the nearby competitor takes almost all the demand and BT drops to about 0. BT’s core extends much further east into the Beitun, Taiping and Xinshe foothills, because there are few other stores in that direction.
Far-away villages are not the lowest. Villages at the northern and southern edges sit in the middle classes (about 0.02-0.03), close to the 1/28 ≈ 0.036 that BT would get if all stores were equally far away. When every store is far, the distances become similar and the probabilities spread out evenly. A village next to a competitor gives BT much less than a remote village does.
Read the quantile legend carefully. With style = "quantile" and n = 10, each colour class holds about 62 villages regardless of the values. Nine classes are squeezed between 0 and 0.067, while the top class spans 0.068-0.944. The map is good for ranking villages, but it makes BT’s influence look much larger than it is. Only about 10% of villages give BT more than 0.07. With fixed breaks (e.g. 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4), only a handful of villages around the store would look dark.
Comparing stores. BT has close competitors: DT about 1.5 km away, and TY and DK both within about 2.3 km. When I changed "BT" to "TG" (the Dajia store in the northwest), the picture was very different. TG has no nearby competitor, so villages up to about 5 km away still give it more than 0.4. BT has a contested trade area, while TG has a captive one. A simple buffer of the same radius around each store would hide this difference.






One use of the Huff model is to estimate store sales from village population. First, we append the P_CNT field from the village sf data.frame to the huff_share data.frame using the code chunk below.

huff_share_pp <- huff_share %>%
  left_join(village %>%
              st_drop_geometry() %>%
              select(VILLCODE, P_CNT),
            by = "VILLCODE") %>%
  relocate(distance, .after = last_col())

Next, shares.total() of the MCI package is used to calculate the total sales, using the code chunk below.

huff_total <- shares.total(huff_share_pp,
                           "VILLCODE",
                           "Store_CD",
                           "p_ij",
                           "P_CNT")







NoteMy understanding: what shares.total() returns



shares.total() implements the slide formulas \(E_{ij} = p_{ij} \times C_i\) and \(T_j = \sum_i E_{ij}\), with \(C_i\) = P_CNT. The output has one row per store:

sum_E_j: the expected number of customers \(T_j\) allocated to that store;
share_j: its market share \(M_j = T_j / \sum T_j\).

Every resident of the 617 villages is allocated to some store, so sum(sum_E_j) equals the total modelled population (about 2.80 million). Strictly speaking, these are expected customers, not sales in dollars. Comparing them with Total_Sales therefore assumes that each resident spends roughly the same amount.


The code chunk below appends the estimated store sales (\(E_j\)) onto the stores sf data.frame.

store_sales_est <- stores %>%
  left_join(huff_total,
            by = join_by("Store_CD" == "suppliers_single"))

Now, we can visualise how well the estimated sales compare with the actual sales using the code chunk below.

store_sales_nongeom <- store_sales_est %>%
  st_drop_geometry()


ggscatterstats(store_sales_nongeom,
               x = sum_E_j,
               y = Total_Sales)














TipMy observation




The relationship is positive and significant: \(\hat r_{Pearson} \approx 0.58\), 95% CI [0.26, 0.78], p ≈ 0.001, with 28 stores. Stores that the model allocates more residents to do tend to sell more.
But location explains only about a third of the variation (\(r^2 \approx 0.33\)). This is expected, because the model only knows distance and competition. Attractiveness is fixed at 100, and \(\lambda\) is not calibrated.
The points below the line are mostly the outer stores. TG (Dajia), SQ (Shengang), ZS (Taiping) and EH (Dongshi) sell much less than their modelled customer totals. The Huff model is a closed system: every resident must choose one of the 28 stores. A lone store in a large rural area is therefore credited with everyone there, even though many of those people will not travel 5-10 km for fast food or will choose another brand. This is the main structural weakness I see in the model.
The points above the line are mostly in the western and central city, e.g. DD (Longjing, toward the industrial park and Tunghai University) and ZK (the Zhong Ke store in Xitun, named after the Central Taiwan Science Park). These areas attract many daytime workers and students, who are not counted in residential P_CNT.
QH is a central store that also sits well below the line, and it has the lowest average bill. This points to a format or operational issue rather than location.

Business takeaway: the gap between observed and modelled sales is more useful than the correlation itself. It separates “poor location” from “good location, weak performance”, and it suggests that daytime population would be a better demand measure than residential population for some stores.


The code chunk below reshapes the Huff probabilities into a wide village-by-store table.

huff_share_wider <- huff_share %>%
  select(VILLCODE, Store_CD, p_ij) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Store_CD,
              values_from = p_ij)







TipMy observation



huff_share_wider is a 617 × 29 table: VILLCODE plus one column per store. Each row adds up to 1. This format is easy to share with a business team, because each row shows how one village’s demand is split across all 28 stores. It also makes it easy to find each village’s dominant store (the column with the highest probability). With equal attractiveness, the dominant store is always the nearest store, so the dominant-store map is effectively a Voronoi diagram of the stores.

title: Market Area Analysis for Retail and Service Locations using Huff model
text:
NoteWhere competition is strongest



From huff_share_wider, I calculated how evenly each village’s probability is spread across stores, using the effective number of competitors \(1/\sum_j p_{ij}^2\). The result surprised me:

Villages right next to a store, even in the dense city core, are close to 1. A store a few hundred metres away gets almost all of that village’s demand under \(d^{-2}\).
The most split villages are in the gaps between stores and across the rural periphery. When every store is far away, the distances are similar, so no single store dominates.

For expansion, these peripheral villages are unclaimed demand: a new store there would become the nearest store and capture most of it. A new store in the core would mostly take customers from other stores in the same franchise.








NoteIs λ = 2 the right distance decay?



The lecture uses MCI’s default lambda = -2, but Lesson 8 stresses that the Huff model should be calibrated. Re-running huff.shares() with different lambda values and comparing modelled shares (share_j) with observed sales shares:

The share error (RMSE) is lowest at about λ = 1, with the default λ = 2 slightly worse.
Larger λ (stronger decay) makes the fit clearly worse, because it gives the isolated outer stores even more of their surrounding villages.

This suggests fast-food customers in Taichung are less distance-sensitive than λ = 2 assumes. One reason could be that people buy near work, school or on the way home, not only near where they live.
This is only a rough check (28 stores, revenue standing in for customers). A proper MCI calibration would regress observed village-level shares on distance and attractiveness after the log-centering transformation. The POD code field in the sales data is a delivery zone, not a village code, so village-level shares cannot be rebuilt from this data.

title: Market Area Analysis for Retail and Service Locations using Huff model
text:
Question
What I learned




What is a Huff trade area?
A continuous probability surface. Trade areas of neighbouring stores overlap, unlike the hard boundaries of Reilly’s law.


What drives the result here?
Only distance and competition. Store_size = 100 cancels out of \(p_{ij}\).


Why check the joins?
The sales file is national. The 5 dropped polygons are non-residential special units, and the 8 unmatched population records are Heping District, which is missing from the boundary layer.


How good is the model?
r ≈ 0.58 with observed sales. It over-credits isolated outer stores and under-credits stores near campuses and workplaces.


What would improve it?
Real attractiveness variables, road travel time instead of straight-line distance, daytime population, and a λ calibrated with MCI on observed shares.

title: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
section: 01 · Research questionWhere does armed conflict concentrate, and is it moving?
text:
01 · Research questionWhere does armed conflict concentrate, and is it moving?

Where do recorded conflict events form significant local clusters, and which township hotspots persist, emerge, intensify or weaken through time?



87,103 ACLED events recorded in the study period


330 Myanmar townships (MIMU Admin-3)


57 monthly time steps, Jan 2021 – Sep 2025


18,810 township-months in a complete space-time cube



Why it matters. Myanmar’s post-2021 conflict is geographically uneven. A national total hides where violence concentrates and how that concentration shifts, which is exactly what peace-building and humanitarian teams need in order to decide where to look first.

title: Geospatial Analytics for Peace

text:
02 · Study area and dataA township-level view of Myanmar, 2021–2025




Total recorded events by township, Jan 2021 – Sep 2025 (quantile classes within each map)




Inputs

ACLED event points: date, type, coordinates, fatalities
MIMU Admin-3 township boundaries, P-code v9.4
Projected working copy in EPSG:6933 for geometry



Data-quality gates

0 duplicate IDs, 0 missing dates or coordinates
1,112 events missing a township name → assigned by coordinates
Only 9 of 87,103 points fall outside any township
Zero-event months kept as observed zeros





The burden is highest in the Sagaing–Magway dry zone (Yinmarbin 3,057 · Salingyi 2,038 · Kale 2,009 events), while battles peak in Shan and Kayin (Nawnghkio 447 · Kawkareik 441) and civilian harm also stands out in Myingyan (Mandalay) and Hpakant (Kachin).

title: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
section: 03 · Analytical approachFrom event points to hotspot trajectories
text:
03 · Analytical approachFrom event points to hotspot trajectories


1 Prepare & match Clean ACLED fields, audit precision, assign every event to a township P-code by spatial join. → township event table


2 Space-time cube Count events per township-month and complete all 330 × 57 combinations. → regular monthly series


3 Local association Local Moran’s I separates clusters from outliers; local Gi* finds high- and low-value concentrations. → LISA & Gi* maps


4 Conflict composition Repeat Gi* for all events, battles and violence against civilians under one rule. → hotspot agreement map


5 Change through time Monthly Gi* maps, Mann-Kendall trends and Emerging Hot Spot Analysis. → EHSA hotspot classes



Weights · Queen contiguity, row-standardised Gi* band · fixed 185.8 km Permutations · 99, seed 626 Decision rule · p < 0.05, with BH-adjusted check Software · R: sf, sfdep, tmap, Kendall



Local Moran’s I asks
Is a township similar to or different from its neighbours? It finds clusters (High-High) and outliers (Low-High).


Local Gi* asks
Is this area a significant concentration of high (hotspot) or low (cold spot) event counts?


EHSA asks
How has each township’s Gi* changed across 57 months: intensifying, oscillating, sporadic or diminishing?

title: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
section: 05 · Public-safety implicationsTurning hotspot types into monitoring priorities
text:
05 · Public-safety implicationsTurning hotspot types into monitoring priorities








Hotspot signal
Recommended response
Why




Recurring recent hotspots
Salingyi, Monywa, Pale, Singu
Sustained township-level review
Hotspot in 7 of the last 12 months: the concentration keeps coming back, it is not a one-off spike.


Intensifying hotspots
Northern & southern Shan, Kawthoung
Field verification and closer monitoring
Local concentration is still rising, so the situation may be getting worse.


Sporadic & oscillating hotspots
Kachin, Rakhine, Bago, Mandalay
Flexible, event-triggered monitoring
Violence disappears and returns, so a fixed long-run ranking would miss flare-ups.


Civilian-harm hotspots
Mandalay, Sagaing, Chin
Protection-focused programming
Recorded violence targets civilians directly, not only armed actors.


Diminishing hotspots
Chipwi, Myitkyina, Pyay
Follow-up before de-prioritising
A falling statistic does not prove that present-day harm is low.




These maps are a screening tool, not a final decision. Field action should also weigh population exposure, displacement, access conditions and consultation with affected communities.

title: Geospatial Analytics for Peace
section: 06 · LimitationsWhat the evidence can and cannot support
text:
06 · LimitationsWhat the evidence can and cannot support


Data
